title: "Introduction to String Art"
unit: 2
cluster: "String Art"

String art is a craft of making patterns by connecting points with thread,
usually around a circle. Every thread is straight, but many threads together
can form curves and intricate patterns.

![Three layers of straight threads form one pattern. [View the program that made it.](https://github.com/anandology/stringart/blob/main/examples/three-circles.py)](/images/stringart-three-circles.svg){fig-alt="A circular string art pattern with three overlapping layers of curved shapes formed entirely from straight lines."}

The craft grew out of *curve stitching*, a technique developed by
[Mary Everest Boole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Everest_Boole) in the
late 1800s to explore geometry by sewing lines on cards. The `stringart` Python
library lets us explore the same idea by connecting numbered points on the
screen.

Small changes to the connections can produce a completely different picture.
That makes string art a useful way to experiment with code: every program
creates something to inspect, and a mistake is often visible in the drawing.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* start a new string art drawing
* connect two numbered points
* add several threads to a drawing
* display the drawing in a notebook

**A string art drawing starts with numbered points. Each call to `connect()`
adds one straight thread between two of those points.**

## Starting a drawing

First import the functions from the `stringart` module:

```{python}
from stringart import *
```

The `*` makes the module's drawing functions available by their short names.
We can call `make_circle()` instead of writing `stringart.make_circle()`.

The `make_circle()` function starts a new drawing. Its argument is the number
of points to place around the circle:

```{python}
make_circle(6)
show()
```

The six points are numbered from `0` to `5`. As with list indexes, the
numbering starts at `0`.

The `show()` function displays the current drawing. There are no threads yet,
so the drawing contains only the numbered points.

Every example below starts with `make_circle()`, so it creates a complete
drawing without depending on an earlier example.

## Connecting two points

The `connect()` function takes two point numbers as arguments. This call adds a
thread from point `0` to point `3`:

```{python}
make_circle(6)

connect(0, 3)

show()
```

Calling `connect()` changes the current drawing. Calling `show()` afterwards
displays that change.

To add several threads to one drawing, call `connect()` several times before
calling `show()`:

```{python}
make_circle(6)

connect(0, 3)
connect(1, 4)
connect(2, 5)

show()
```

The three threads connect opposite points on the circle. They meet at the
centre even though no point was placed there.

## Connecting every second point

The next drawing connects each point to the point two positions ahead:

```{python}
make_circle(6)
connect(0, 2)
connect(2, 4)
connect(4, 6)
show()
```

These three connections form a triangle. The circle has points `0` to `5`, but
the last call uses point `6`. Point numbers wrap around the circle, so point `6`
is point `0` again. Therefore, `connect(4, 6)` closes the triangle by connecting
point `4` to point `0`.

Starting with the odd-numbered points produces another triangle. Both triangles
can be part of the same drawing:

```{python}
make_circle(6)

# top triangle
connect(0, 2)
connect(2, 4)
connect(4, 6)

# bottom triangle
connect(1, 3)
connect(3, 5)
connect(5, 7)

show()
```

Together, the two triangles form a six-pointed star. Every call follows the
same rule: connect a point to the point two positions ahead. This rule can later
be written as `connect(i, i+2)`, without treating the last connection as a
special case.

## Practice

### Problem 1

Write python code to make the pattern shown below.

```{python}
#| echo: false
make_circle(5)
for i in range(5):
    connect(i, i+1)
show()
```

### Problem 2

Write python code to make the pattern shown below.

```{python}
#| echo: false
make_circle(5)
for i in range(5):
    connect(i, i+2)
show()
```

### Problem 3


Write python code to make the pattern shown below.

```{python}
#| echo: false

make_circle(8)

connect(0, 2)
connect(2, 4)
connect(4, 6)
connect(6, 8)

connect(1, 5)
connect(3, 7)

show()
```


## Summary

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `from stringart import *` | makes the String Art drawing functions available by their short names |
| `make_circle(6)` | starts a new string art drawing with `6` points, numbered from `0` to `5` |
| `connect(0, 3)` | adds a straight thread between points `0` and `3` |
| `connect(4, 6)` with six points | connects point `4` to point `0` because point numbers wrap around |
| several calls to `connect()` | add several threads to the current drawing |
| `show()` | displays the current drawing in a notebook |

And the one idea to carry forward: a string art pattern is built one thread at
a time by connecting numbered points.
